reading.rtitle: Two Futures That Could Not Both Happen
paras: Beatriz Nunes spent the whole of last year preparing for two futures that could not both happen. In the morning she studied for a national exam that eighty thousand people take for four hundred places. In the evening she wrote application essays for universities four thousand miles away. Her friends called it hedging. She called it arithmetic. “If I only prepare for one outcome,” she says, “I am not being confident. I am just refusing to look at the likelihood.”

The word she uses for the second plan is contingency, and she is precise about what it does not mean. A contingency is not a lesser thing you would settle for. It is a second real plan, prepared to the same standard, which exists because nobody controls which door opens. “If I get the place here, I will stay, and I will be happy. In the event that I do not, I will go, and I will also be happy. That is the whole design. Neither scenario is the sad one.”

What she found hardest was not the work. It was the second kind of sentence, the one that begins with if I weren’t. Saying out loud a life she is not living, in front of people who love her, felt to her like giving up. It took months to see it differently. “If I weren’t doing this, I would probably be working and studying at night,” she says now, without flinching. “Saying it does not make it happen. It only means I have looked at it, and I can tell you whether it is realistic.”

She got the place. She is in her first semester, and she still keeps the other file on her desktop, unopened. When somebody asks whether the essays were wasted, she is quick. “It all depends on what you think I was buying. I was not buying a second university. I was buying the ability to walk into that exam without being afraid of the result, and that is what let me pull it off.” Before any of it, she spent a month on what she calls the feasibility question: not what would be wonderful, but what she could actually envision herself doing for six years.
reading.source: A composite portrait of a two-track application year, written for this lesson.

items.situation: Say what will happen if Beatriz gets the place, in one sentence.
tips: If she gets the place, she will stay and she will be happy.
Real and likely, so present simple after if, and will after the comma.

items.situation: Now say what she would do if she could choose any city in the world.
tips: If she could choose any city, she would probably study abroad.
Imagined, so the verb steps back and will becomes would.

items.situation: Correct this out loud: If I will pass, I will move.
tips: If I pass, I will move.
Never will inside the if half. This is the number one error from Portuguese.

items.situation: Give advice with If I were you, about anything you like.
tips: If I were you, I would apply to both.
Were for every person, not was, when the sentence is imagined.

items.situation: Say what you will do if the result in January is good.
tips: If I get in, I will move closer to the university.
Real and likely: present simple after if.

items.situation: Now say what you would be doing right now if none of this had started.
tips: If I were not studying for this, I would probably be training every day.
Imagined, so were, and would plus the bare verb after the comma.

listenings.text: So people keep asking me how I did two applications at once, and honestly the answer is boring. I put them in different halves of the day and I stopped arguing with myself about it. The part nobody warns you about is the emotional one. If you tell somebody you are also applying abroad, half of them hear that you do not believe you will get in here. And if I am completely honest, for about two months I thought the same thing myself. What changed was one sentence a teacher said to me. She said a contingency is not a prediction. Writing the second plan does not make the first one less likely. It only means that in the event that the first door does not open, you are not standing in a corridor in January with nothing in your hands.

I have spent fifteen years asking people why they did not have a second plan, and the answers are almost always the same three. The first is that it feels like bad luck, as if naming the outcome could somehow cause it. The second is that it looks like weakness in front of other people, which matters more than anybody admits. The third one is the interesting one. They say they did not have the time. But when we look at what they actually did with those hours, the second plan would have cost about four per cent of the total. So it is not time. It is that thinking about the losing scenario is unpleasant, and the mind is extremely good at finding a respectable reason to avoid something unpleasant. My advice has not changed in fifteen years. Do not ask yourself whether you will fail. Ask what you would do on the Monday afterwards. That question is answerable, and once it is answered it stops taking up room.
